procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Collector of Customs confiscating goods and imposing a penalty of Rs. 1,000 on the petitioner.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The petitioner preferred an appeal to the Central Board of Revenue, which was dismissed as being filed out of time. The petitioner then made an application to the Government of India for revision of the order of the Central Board of Revenue.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution of India for enforcement of Fundamental Rights, challenging the validity of the order of the Collector of Customs.

directions: The application is dismissed with costs.
The appeal is dismissed with costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the portion of Section 3(2) of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947, which substitutes the word 'shall' with 'may' in Section 183 of the Sea Customs Act, grants uncontrolled discretion to the Customs authorities and thereby violates Article 14 of the Constitution.

facts: The petitioner's goods were confiscated under Section 167, item 8, of the Sea Customs Act, 1878, for being imported in violation of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947.
The petitioner was not given an option to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation.

The petitioner argued that the portion of Section 3(2) of the 1947 Act, which changes the word "shall" to "may" in Section 183 of the Sea Customs Act, grants uncontrolled discretion to customs authorities, thereby violating Article 14 of the Constitution.

law.description: This section applies the provisions of the Sea Customs Act, 1878, to goods whose import is controlled by the 1947 Act. It specifically modifies Section 183 of the Sea Customs Act by substituting the mandatory word "shall" with the discretionary word "may".
This section deals with the option to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation. As originally written, it mandated ("shall") that an officer give the owner this option.
This is the provision that authorizes the confiscation of illegally imported goods.
Guarantees equality before the law and protects against arbitrary or uncontrolled discretion by the state.

application.description: The Court first determined that Section 3(2) of the 1947 Act does not, by its own force, grant any discretion to the customs authorities. Its sole purpose is to make the Sea Customs Act applicable to certain cases.
The Court stated that a statute which only applies another statute to a set of cases cannot, in itself, be said to violate Article 14.
The Court then addressed the petitioner's argument by assuming, for the sake of argument, that the *modified* Section 183 (which now contained the word "may") did violate Article 14.

The Court reasoned that even if the modified Section 183 were unconstitutional, it would not help the petitioner. The power to confiscate the goods does not come from Section 183. The confiscation was authorized and carried out under a different provision, Section 167, item 8, of the Sea Customs Act.
The Court clarified that Section 183 only comes into play *after* a confiscation has been adjudged, by providing an option to pay a fine. It does not authorize the confiscation itself.

Therefore, even if the modified Section 183 were to be struck down entirely, the original order of confiscation made under Section 167 would remain valid. The petitioner's challenge was aimed at the confiscation order, and this line of reasoning did not invalidate it.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's argument, holding that Section 3(2) of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947, does not itself offend Article 14 because it does not grant any discretion. Furthermore, even if the resulting modified version of Section 183 of the Sea Customs Act were unconstitutional, it would not invalidate the confiscation order, as the power to confiscate stems from a different and valid section of the law (Section 167, item 8).

issue.issue_text: Whether the petitioner was denied an opportunity of being heard on the question of whether an option to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation should be given.

facts: The petitioner received a show-cause notice from the Customs authorities asking why his goods should not be confiscated.
The petitioner did not appear at the hearing.
The petitioner had previously been asked if he wanted a personal hearing and had replied that he did not.
application: The Court reasoned that the notice to show cause against confiscation inherently included the possibility that the confiscation could be absolute, without an option to pay a fine.
This notice, therefore, served as the petitioner's opportunity to appear and argue why the confiscation should not be absolute and why he should be given the option to pay a fine.
The Court placed the fault on the petitioner for not availing himself of the opportunity that had been provided.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's argument, holding that he had been given an opportunity to be heard on the matter through the show-cause notice but had failed to take advantage of it.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Customs authority erred by considering other transactions without giving notice to the petitioner when deciding not to grant an option to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation.

facts: The petitioner argued that the Customs authority, when deciding not to grant him the option to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation, considered certain other transactions.
The petitioner claimed he was not given any notice that these other transactions would be considered, nor was he given an opportunity to be heard regarding them.
law: A show-cause notice asking why goods should not be confiscated inherently includes the possibility that the confiscation order might be absolute, without an option to pay a fine.
application: The Supreme Court found that the initial show-cause notice given to the petitioner was sufficient.
This notice necessarily informed the petitioner that an order for confiscation could be made without giving him the option to pay a fine.
Therefore, the petitioner had the opportunity to appear at the hearing and argue why the confiscation should not be absolute and why he should be granted the option to pay a fine.
reasoning.conclusion: The Court rejected the petitioner's argument, concluding that it was his own fault for not availing himself of the opportunity to be heard that was provided by the initial show-cause notice. Since the notice covered the possibility of an absolute confiscation, no separate notice regarding the consideration of other transactions was necessary.

issue.issue_text: Whether the transaction involving the managing agency was a sale or transfer, or a relinquishment.

facts: The case involved a transaction concerning a managing agency.
The facts and circumstances of the transaction were presented to the court in an agreed statement of the case.
application: The Supreme Court examined the "true legal character" of the transaction.
The Court determined that the transaction was a relinquishment of the managing agency.
The Court explicitly found that the transaction was neither a sale nor a transfer of the managing agency.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the transaction was a relinquishment, not a sale or transfer. It, therefore, affirmed the decision of the High Court of Bombay and dismissed the appeal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the portion of Section 3(2) of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947, which substitutes the word 'shall' with 'may' in Section 183 of the Sea Customs Act, grants uncontrolled discretion to the Customs authorities and thereby violates Article 14 of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The substitution of 'shall' with 'may' grants uncontrolled discretion to the Customs authorities to decide whether to offer an option to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation.
This uncontrolled discretion violates Article 14 of the Constitution.
The offending portion of Section 3(2) should be struck down.
Consequently, Section 183 of the Sea Customs Act should apply without modification, making it obligatory for the authorities to offer a fine.
Since no such obligatory option was given, the confiscation order is invalid.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a statute applies the provisions of another Act with a specific modification, the modified provision is considered a single, indivisible statutory provision. If this modified provision is challenged as unconstitutional, it must be invalidated as a whole; it is not permissible to sever only the modification to revert to the original, unmodified text of the provision.
obiter: A confiscation order may be justified under other provisions of the Sea Customs Act that authorize confiscation, without needing to resort to Section 183, which merely provides for an option to pay a fine in lieu of a confiscation already adjudged.

The court made no determination on whether Section 183 of the Sea Customs Act, as modified by the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947, actually offends Article 14 of the Constitution, as it was not necessary for the decision.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that Section 3(2) of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947, which modifies Section 183 of the Sea Customs Act by changing 'shall' to 'may', does not violate Article 14 of the Constitution because the provision itself does not grant discretion, it only modifies another statute. Even if the modified Section 183 were unconstitutional, it would be struck down in its entirety, which would not help the petitioner, as the power to confiscate stems from Section 167, not Section 183. Furthermore, the Customs authorities did not act improperly, as the petitioner declined a hearing and the decision not to offer a fine was reasonably based on the petitioner's deliberate violation of import laws.
legal_tests_applied: Severability Test: When assessing a statutory provision modified by another act, the court considers it a single, indivisible provision. If found unconstitutional, it must be struck down as a whole, not just the modifying part. The court stated, 'Section 183 with or without the modification really contains one statutory provision and therefore it must go out of the statute book as a whole or not at all.'

Test for Arbitrary Discretion under Article 14: Discretion is not considered uncontrolled or unreasonable if it is vested in high officers, subject to appeal, guided by the objective of the statute, and its exercise is a quasi-judicial act based on the gravity of the offense. The court noted, 'the discretion is vested in high Customs officers and there are appeals from their order. The imposition of the fine is really a quasi-judicial act and the test of the quantum of it is in the gravity of the offence. The object of the Act is to prevent unauthorised importation of goods and the discretion has to be exercised with that object in view.'
why_appellant_lost: The argument that Section 3(2) of the 1947 Act grants uncontrolled discretion failed because the court found that 'Bv its own force . no part of s. 3(2) purports to give any discretion to the Custom:r-authorities at all.' Its only effect is to modify Section 183.

The argument that the unconstitutional part of the law should be severed failed because the court held that the modified Section 183 is a single provision; if it offends Article 14, it 'goes out as a whole,' leaving no obligation to offer a fine.

The petitioner's claim that the confiscation order was invalid without an option to pay a fine was rejected because the power to confiscate comes from Section 167, item 8, of the Sea Customs Act, and 'Resort to s. 183 of the Sea Customs Act is not necessary to justify the order of confiscation made in this case at all.'

The claim of being denied a hearing was factually incorrect, as 'the petitioner had been asked before the order was made whether he wanted a personal hearing and he had stated in reply that he did not... He had been given an opportUnity and had not availed himself of it.'

The argument that the show-cause notice was insufficient was rejected because the notice 'to show cause 'why the goods should not be confiscated also informed him necessarily that an order for confiscation might be made without an option to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation being given'.

The challenge to the authorities considering other transactions was dismissed because their conclusion was reasonable. The petitioner had prior notice that the goods were prohibited, and 'It was not unreasonable for the Customs-authorities to think that the petitioner had deliberately imported the goods in breach of the order . of the Government... and on that ground to think it proper not to give him the option.'
why_respondent_won: The respondent prevailed on the constitutionality issue because the court agreed that Section 3(2) of the 1947 Act does not itself confer discretion and is therefore not unconstitutional. The power to confiscate was independently and validly exercised under Section 167.
The respondent's position that a proper hearing was offered was upheld, as the court found evidence that the petitioner was offered a personal hearing and explicitly declined it.

The respondent's decision not to offer an option to pay a fine was deemed a valid exercise of discretion, justified by the court on the grounds that the petitioner had knowingly and deliberately imported prohibited goods after being warned not to.

The court accepted that the show-cause notice for confiscation implicitly covered the possibility that no option to pay a fine would be given, thereby placing the onus on the petitioner to argue for such an option.
policy_considerations: The court shows deference to administrative discretion when it is vested in high-ranking officials and is subject to an appellate process, viewing these as safeguards against arbitrariness.

The court affirmed that administrative discretion is not uncontrolled when it must be exercised in line with the stated objectives of the governing statute, in this case, the prevention of unauthorized importation of goods.
